definition: Pillage means to rob a place violently, especially in war.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pillage. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pillage should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Norse raiders pillaged the island abbey in a single tide, carrying off the plate, the relics, and the winter grain.
A swipe is theft at its smallest — one item, palmed on the sly, with no force at all — where pillage is theft at the scale of a town, taken by open force.
Loot goes further than swipe — armfuls carried out of the disorder — but pillage claims the most: a place stripped wholesale, by force, down to its stores.

To ransack is to tear one place apart in a rough, violent search — a house, a shop, a single desk — hunting for whatever is worth taking. Pillage is bigger and blunter: an army stripping a whole town of its goods by force, no searching required.

To plunder is to strip a place of its valuables by open force — the victor's haul, the raider's right — and the word can even name the goods themselves. Pillage is its war-zone twin: always the violent act of robbing a town, never the goods.

French piller, "to plunder," has no proven parent — the guesses run from a Latin verb for stripping hair to an old word for rag — and it left no other everyday English word. One caution: the pill from the pharmacy is Latin pilula, "little ball," and no relation at all.
Pillage means to rob a place violently, especially in war.
In August of 410, Alaric's Goths spent three days pillaging Rome.

They worked with terrifying speed and order: gold from the temples, silver from the great houses, grain wagons from the riverside warehouses — but they burned little and battered less, and on the fourth day they marched out with the city still standing behind them.
Pillage is the exact word for those three days, because it means to rob a place violently, especially in war — and robbery is the whole of it.
Pillaging armies take; what they leave is emptied, not leveled.
Loot is its street-scale cousin; ransack is the rough search of one house.
Pillage is theft at the scale of towns — and its unit-mate raze is what happens when the army wants nothing left at all.
Pillage lives in war reporting and history: armies pillage, and what they take is the point.
Loot fits civil disorder; ransack, a single violent search.
Keep the unit's line bright — pillage is theft, raze is demolition.
A pillaged town is poorer; a razed one is gone.

The ledger of the cloth merchant Anna Vogel is one of the few records to survive the sack of her city in 1633.
Its early pages are all business -- dyes bought, bolts sold -- but the entries from that October read like testimony.
A passing army, unpaid for months, was turned loose on the town for two days to pillage it in place of wages.
Vogel lists what was taken from her street alone: forty bolts of wool, the smith's tools, every horse but one lame mare.
Her last October entry is a single line -- nothing left to enter -- and the ledger stays blank until spring.
